content: Positional plagiocephaly, also referred to as deformational plagiocephaly or flat head syndrome, is a condition predominantly observed in infants. It is characterized by the development of a flattened area on the back or one side of the head, which occurs due to prolonged periods of lying in a single position. This condition can arise from torticollis, a situation where the neck muscles on one side of the head develop asymmetrically, causing the head to tilt to one side. However, more commonly, it occurs in otherwise healthy infants who sleep in the same position for extended durations. In 1992, the American Academy of Pediatrics introduced the Back to Sleep campaign, which advised parents to place their infants on their backs during sleep instead of their stomachs, as was previously recommended. This initiative successfully reduced the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) by nearly 40%. However, it also led to a 600% increase in the incidence of positional plagiocephaly. The prognosis for positional plagiocephaly is excellent, and in most cases, the condition can be reversed before the child reaches one year of age. Treatment approaches can be as straightforward as occasionally repositioning the infant's head during sleep and increasing the amount of supervised tummy time. In severe cases, specially designed helmets may be used to help reshape the skull. Once the child begins to move independently, the condition often improves rapidly on its own. Importantly, while the flattening of the head may appear concerning, it typically does not harm the brain or impede its development. A similar but distinct condition, craniosynostosis, occurs when the bones of the skull fuse prematurely. Unlike positional plagiocephaly, craniosynostosis is a more serious condition that necessitates surgical intervention.
